senses.d: A single aspect of a given thing.
ex: This film can be enjoyed on many dimensions - the script is great, the acting is realistic, and the special effects will simply take you aback.

senses.d: A measure of spatial extent in a particular direction, such as height, width or breadth, or depth.
A construct whereby objects or individuals can be distinguished.
The number of independent coordinates needed to specify uniquely the location of a point in a space; also, any of such independent coordinates.
The number of elements of any basis of a vector space.
One of the physical properties that are regarded as fundamental measures of a physical quantity, such as mass, length and time.
ex: The dimension of velocity is length divided by time.

senses.d: Any of the independent ranges of indices in a multidimensional array.
A universe or plane of existence.
ex: a machine that lets you travel to a parallel dimension.
He was experimenting with matter transportation through the nth dimension.

senses.d: To mark, cut or shape something to specified dimensions.
ex: The first sixty argam form the basis for my own sexagesimal use, in the accounting of my business and in the dimensioning of buildings.

senses.d: To specify the size of (an array or similar data structure); to allocate.
ex: Dimension an array to hold only as much data as you intend to put into it.

From Middle English dime, from Anglo-Norman disme (“one tenth, tithe”) (modern French dîme), from Medieval Latin decima, from Latin decima (pars) (“tenth (part)”). Doublet of decim, decima, and decime.
From the use of the coin in a payphone to report a crime to the police. US payphones charged 10¢ in almost all jurisdictions until the late 1970s.

senses.d: A coin worth one-tenth of a dollar, that is, ten cents.
A small amount of money.
ex: She didn't spend a dime.

senses.d: An assist.
A playing card with the rank of ten.
Ten dollars.
A thousand dollars.
ex: At one point, Rob hit a dire losing streak. In a single week, he dropped a dime—$1,000.

senses.d: A measure of illicit drugs (usually marijuana) sold in ten-dollar bags.
A ten-year prison sentence.
ex: These deaths got him a dime in a minimum-security prison.

senses.d: Payment responsibility.
ex: Are you traveling on the company's dime?

senses.d: A beautiful woman (10 on a 10-point scale).
ex: Make a couple of nuns a couple of dimes.
Wait in line for drinks, it’s another time out / Made out on the floor with a couple dimes

senses.d: To inform on, to turn in to the authorities, to rat on, especially anonymously.
ex: Somebody dimed on me and I got arrested for selling marijuana.

senses.d: To operate an audio amplifier (especially an electric guitar amplifier) at level "10" (typically the highest amplification level).
ex: I get the best-sounding sustain and smooth harmonic distortion when I run the amp dimed.

From Middle English dim, dym, from Old English dim, dimm (“dim, dark, gloomy; wretched, grievous, sad, unhappy”), from Proto-West Germanic *dimm, from Proto-Germanic *dimmaz (“dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰem- (“to whisk, smoke; obscure”). Compare Faroese dimmur (“dark”), Icelandic dimmur (“dark”) and dimma (“darkness”).

senses.d: Not bright or colorful.
ex: The lighting was too dim for me to make out his facial features.
that sustaining Love / Which, through the web of being blindly wove / By man and beast and earth and air and sea, / Burns bright or dim

senses.d: Not smart or intelligent.
ex: He may be a bit dim, but he's not entirely stupid.

senses.d: Indistinct, hazy or unclear.
ex: His vision grew dimmer as he aged.

senses.d: Disapproving, unfavorable: rarely used outside the phrase take a dim view of.
Dimness.
To make something less bright.
ex: He dimmed the lights and put on soft music.

senses.d: To become darker.
ex: The lights dimmed briefly when the air conditioning was turned on.

senses.d: To render dim, obscure, or dark; to make less bright or distinct.
ex: a king among his courtiers,[…] who out to dim the lustre of all his attendants
Now ſet the ſun, and twilight dimm'd the ways, […]

senses.d: To deprive of distinct vision; to hinder from seeing clearly, either by dazzling or clouding the eyes; to darken the senses or understanding of.
ex:
And with our Sun-bright armour as we march,
Weel chaſe the Starrs from heauen, and dim their eies
That ſtand and muſe at our admyred armes.
Her starry eyes were dimm'd with streaming tears.

senses.d: To diminish, dull, or curtail.
ex: All these setbacks had started to dim the hopes of the students.
Nothing will dim their spirit of resilience.
